sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL8021.M68 S465 2011
sources.note: Emakhuwa chapter pp. 70-82: Esaaka listed as a variant spoken in Eráti, Nacarôa, part of Memba (Nampula) and Chiúre, Mecúfi (Cabo Delgado); 'Tom: Emakhuwa é uma língua tonal.'; no stress statement for Emakhuwa; bibliography p. 82 cites Afido 1988 (LIMANI N.4) and Katupha 1983 (unpublished M.Phil.).

sources.citation: van der Wal, Jenneke. 2009. Word order and information structure in Makhuwa-Enahara. Utrecht: LOT (LOT 215). PhD thesis, Leiden University.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Enahara variety (Ilha de Moçambique), not Esaaka. p. 20: 'Makhuwa does not have automatic penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde.'; sec. 2.2.2 p. 34: 'Unlike these languages, Makhuwa does not have this penultimate lengthening.'; describes Makhuwa as tonal; p. 17 names 'Katupha (1983, 1991) on Makhuwa-Esaaka'; no word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Kroger, Oliver. 2005. Report on a survey of coastal Makua dialects. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2005-020. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Esaaka is a coastal Makhuwa dialect (Erati, Memba, Chiúre, Mecúfi); an SIL survey report may include phonological notes on Esaaka/Saka.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. 2003. Makhuwa (P30). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 546-565. London: Routledge.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 547 locates Esaaka in 'coastal regions of Cabo Delgado and Nampula provinces'; p. 548 says Katupha's 1983 M.Phil. 'provides an excellent overview of the morphological structure of the Esaaka dialect'; sec. 3.4 tone: 'In the Esaaka dialect, there is no general doubling..'; the word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the chapter; no stress or penultimate-lengthening statement.

sources.citation: Cassimjee, Farida & Charles W. Kisseberth. 1999. A conspiracy argument for Optimality Theory: Emakhuwa dialectology. U. Penn Working Papers in Linguistics 6(1): 81-96.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 5 'Esaaka' (pp. 87-88) and sec. 7 treat only High Tone Doubling in Esaaka, conditioned by IP-penult / IP-final position; 'accent' occurs only as 'acute accent' = H-tone mark; no statement about word stress or penultimate lengthening.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. & Rozenn Guérois. 2019. Makhuwa (P30). In Mark Van de Velde, Koen Bostoen, Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.
